In August, the PCE fell short of expectations, prompting Goldman Sachs to push back its rate hike to December, and market pricing adjusted accordingly; however, a substantial upward revision to GDP underscores economic resilience, while inflation trends have shown only limited improvement. According to Woofun AI, Goldman Sachs (GS.US), based on August personal consumption expenditures (PCE) data and the latest remarks by New York Fed President John Williams, has officially pushed back its expectation for the Federal Reserve's second rate hike this year from October to December, while noting that the likelihood of ultimately needing no further rate hikes has increased significantly. This revision in the forecast marks a significant shift on Wall Street regarding the trajectory of monetary policy. The underlying rationale is that recent inflation indicators have failed to sustain their earlier improvement, while market‑based measures have remained steady around 3% both before and after the statistical methodology change—still well above the Fed's 2% target. "The New Fed News Agency" columnist Nick Timiraos notes that despite strong readings in June and July, August's data showed no continuation of the disinflationary trend. Coupled with earlier weak PPI and CPI figures, the market had already anticipated this development; thus, the PCE data did not deliver any game‑changing insights but rather confirmed the reality that inflation has been stuck at elevated levels since April 2025, failing to make progress toward the 2% target. Goldman Sachs' economics team, led by Jan Hatzius, explicitly noted in its report that the core PCE price index rose 0.25% month-over-month and 3.01% year-over-year—well below market expectations. This prompted them to lower their forecast for fourth-quarter core PCE year-over-year growth to 3%, a figure significantly below the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) participants' median projection of 3.4%, thereby reinforcing the view that rate hikes will be paused in October and action may not resume until December. At the analyst level, differing institutions exhibit significant divergence in their interpretations of inflationary pressures, reflecting market uncertainty over the timing of a policy pivot. Stephen Brown, Chief North American Economist at Capital Economics, adopts a relatively dovish stance, arguing that core price pressures are slightly less severe than previously feared and supporting the view that the Fed will pause rate hikes in October. He specifically notes that the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)'s recent revision to the PCE methodology has led to downward revisions in historical core inflation data, with these adjustments collectively reducing core inflation by roughly 0.3 percentage points. Coupled with the downward revisions for June and July, this brings the annualized pace of core inflation over the past three months down to 2%, providing statistical support for a pause in rate increases. However, Sal Guatieri, a senior economist at BMO (BMO.US), offered a more cautious assessment, arguing that the underlying trend in inflation has not shown any substantial improvement. According to data compiled by Woofun AI, although the share of PCE price components with annualized increases exceeding 3% has declined from 54% to 51%, it remains well above normal levels—hardly enough to suggest that the fundamental inflationary trend has been fundamentally reversed. Guatieri emphasized that this structural pressure will reinforce the Federal Reserve's view that further policy tightening is still needed to bring inflation back to its target, thereby offsetting some of the easing expectations stemming from the recent cooling of short-term data. This divergence highlights the complexity of current inflation data: on the one hand, the deceleration in month-over-month growth provides some breathing room; on the other hand, the year-on-year base effect and persistent structural components of high inflation continue to pose a dilemma for policymakers. Market pricing has swiftly captured this subtle shift in policy expectations, yet volatility remains pronounced. According to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool, the market currently assigns roughly a 39% probability to a rate hike in October, down from about 45% prior to the release of the PCE data, indicating that investors have scaled back their bets on the near-term pace of monetary tightening. Meanwhile, the probability of a rate hike in December has surged to 90%, signaling that the market has clearly pushed back the window for tightening. In the bond market, the yield on the 2-year U.S. Treasury note fell sharply from 4.887% to around 4.864% following the release of the PCE data, directly reflecting investors' waning expectations regarding the urgency of near-term Fed rate hikes. However, this downward trend did not persist; yields subsequently rebounded, fully reversing their earlier decline, underscoring that market concerns about persistent long-term inflation remain. Meanwhile, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield continued to rise, further confirming that long-term interest rates are driven by both economic resilience and inflation expectations. This dynamic shift in the yield curve suggests that, despite a decline in the probability of near-term rate hikes, the market has not yet pivoted fully to an easing bias. Instead, it has repriced both the terminal level and the pace of the hiking cycle, underscoring continued respect for the Fed's "higher for longer" policy stance. The robust resilience of macroeconomic fundamentals provides a solid underpinning for inflationary stickiness, making it difficult for the Federal Reserve to pivot easily toward easing. U.S. second-quarter GDP growth was sharply revised up to an annualized 2.2%, well above the previously reported 1.5%, signaling economic momentum that far exceeded expectations. Both consumption and investment—two key components—outperformed their prior readings; in particular, the critical measure of endogenous growth momentum—real private domestic final sales—was also revised upward to 4.6%, underscoring strong domestic demand. The upward revision in investment largely reflects the boost to growth from AI‑related infrastructure spending, while the higher estimate for consumer spending indicates that, supported by a resilient labor market and a buoyant stock market, households' financial conditions remain broadly sound. In August, consumer spending rose 0.9% month over month, partly driven by higher gasoline expenditures amid rising oil prices, while income growth edged down slightly from 0.3% last month to 0.2%. Meanwhile, the overall PCE price index increased 3.4% year over year, unchanged from the previous month, with month‑over‑month growth accelerating to 0.3%. This set of data indicates that, although the deceleration in the month-over-month growth of the PCE has reduced the urgency of a rate hike in October, robust economic expansion and resilient consumer spending suggest that inflationary pressures will not ease quickly. Consequently, the Federal Reserve must remain cautious in balancing growth and inflation, as any premature easing could heighten the risk of an inflationary rebound. title: 2027 Federal Pay Freeze: How Are 2027 GS Pay Scales with Locality Calculated? - fedagent.com
content: The end of the calendar year often brings updates to General Schedule (GS) Pay Scales for the Federal workforce.  Here’s an in-depth look at the essential details for 2027 to help you navigate your compensation and make informed decisions for your financial future. On August 26, 2026, President Trump officially submitted an alternative pay plan. This proposal includes a pay freeze on both base and locality pay for most Civilian Federal Employees. The proposal cited fiscal responsibility and economic conditions. The planned pay freeze does make an exception for Federal law enforcement, proposing a 3.8% raise starting in January, as well as service members, with a 5-7% raise for active military and 3.6% pay increase for other uniformed service members. The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) will determine which law enforcement positions are eligible for the 3.8% raise next year. Federal employees received a 1% base pay raise in 2026, after an initial proposed pay raise, but no locality pay raise. The proposed pay freeze would also leave locality pay unchanged from 2026. There are currently 53 locality pay areas. The United States Office of Personnel Management (OPM) uses three factors to calculate GS pay scales. This system applies to most Civilian Feds under the General Schedule, excluding those covered by Executive and Senior Level Pay Tables. The GS Pay Grade system includes 15 categories of pay ranges. GS-1 is the lowest, and GS-15 is the highest. Jobs are assigned a grade based on the level of responsibility, qualifications, and experience. For example, a position that requires a high school diploma but no experience in that field may be a GS-2 position. A position that requires a master’s degree is usually a GS-9. The GS Pay Step system divides each pay grade into 10 steps. Each step is worth about 3% of the employee’s salary, so the higher the step, the higher the salary. Promotions and seniority-based milestones lead to higher steps. In general, it takes 18 years to move from the lowest to the highest step within a single grade. Locality relates to the region where the employee works. This factor adjusts the base rate of pay for the cost of living in a geographic area. While each position is assigned to a specific grade, and each employee is assigned to a step within that grade, the pay rate will vary by location. This ensures fair compensation in high-cost areas like California or major metropolitan areas. While the system may seem complicated, these three factors help address the most fundamental questions involved in compensating a workforce: ·       The differences between positions in terms of responsibilities, difficulties, requirements, etc. ·       The need to compensate long-term workers for their service. ·       The cost-of-living differences when the workforce is located all over the country. Of the three determining factors, locality adjustments can be the most complicated to predict. The amount of the adjustment is calculated as a percentage rate based on data from the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics Annual National Compensation Survey. This tool gathers data on compensation from government and non-government sectors in locations all over the country. This information is then compared to the base pay of federal employees in similar positions to calculate the locality pay adjustment factor. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) defines 53 locality areas that OPM uses in setting locality adjustments for all 50 states and all United States territories and possessions. OMB uses defined Metropolitan Statistical Areas and Combined Statistical Areas for this purpose. Hawaii and Alaska have their own pay scales, and 51 other locality areas center on major metropolitan areas. Locations inside the continental United States that don’t fall into an established locality area are grouped as “Rest of United States.” Year over year, OPM recommends changes as needed. The President recommends wholesale adjustments to the pay scales, and they are then approved by Congress each year. Federal employees working abroad are not eligible for locality pay adjustments. How Can I Use the Locality Pay Adjustment Factor Information? Civilian Feds often earn more because of the locality pay adjustment factor. You can find the adjustment rate for your locality by visiting the locality area pay definitions published by OPM. This tool is also useful if you’re considering applying for a similar position in a different part of the country; you can estimate how much higher or lower the pay might be in a new location. title: GS E&C completes land-based salmon farming trial - The Korea Herald
content:
Business GS E&C completes land-based salmon farming trial Busan facility reuses up to 99% of farming water, with full-scale shipments set to begin this year GS Engineering & Construction has completed a trial of its land-based Atlantic salmon farming operation, using its water treatment technology to build expertise for future aquaculture projects. Its subsidiary Eco Aquafarm marked the milestone with a ceremony at the Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster in Gijang County on Wednesday. GS E&C CEO Huh Yoon-hong attended alongside officials from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and the Busan Metropolitan Government. Eco Aquafarm has managed the full production cycle, from hatching fertilized eggs to raising and shipping salmon. The facility combines a recirculating aquaculture system with digital monitoring and Zero Water Concept technology to reuse up to 99 percent of its farming water. Farming Atlantic salmon requires precise control of temperature, salinity and dissolved oxygen as the fish transition between freshwater and seawater. Heat exchangers and precision controls keep water temperatures at 12-16 degrees Celsius during summer, while a central monitoring system tracks water quality and equipment in real time. The company has applied for a patent for an underwater camera system that helps determine when salmon are ready to move to the next growth stage. GS E&C and Eco Aquafarm secured patents for recirculating aquaculture facilities in 2023 and desalination aquaculture facilities in 2025. To strengthen food safety and quality control, Eco Aquafarm completed seafood traceability and HACCP registration last year and obtained antibiotic-free certification for its Atlantic salmon in June. The companies are also working with LG Electronics to improve hygiene at land-based farms and with the National Institute of Fisheries Science on aquatic disease research and preventive vaccines. GS E&C plans to use the technology, operating experience and data gathered in Busan to expand into other land-based aquaculture projects. “We have accumulated the technologies and operational capabilities needed across the entire land-based aquaculture process, from water treatment and fish cultivation to facility operation, by raising Atlantic salmon at the Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster,” a GS E&C official said. Completed in December 2024, the cluster has an annual production capacity of 500 tons of Atlantic salmon. GS E&C participates as a private-sector operator through Eco Aquafarm, which plans to begin full-scale shipments later this year. Eco Aquafarm, a subsidiary established by GS E&C for land-based salmon farming, held a ceremony Wednesday to mark the successful completion of the demonstration project and showcased Atlantic salmon raised at Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster ahead of commercial shipments. GS E&C CEO Huh Yoon-hong and officials from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and Busan city government attended the event, and tasted the land-raised salmon and were briefed on the company’s farming technologies. The cluster is a testbed facility capable of producing up to 500 tons of Atlantic salmon annually, with commercial shipments set to begin by the end of this year Eco Aquafarm was established in 2020 to develop a new business leveraging builder GS E&C’s water treatment technologies. Since then, the subsidiary has operated the entire farming process, from incubating Atlantic salmon eggs and raising fish, managing water quality and shipments. Eco Aquafarm's facility at Busan Smart Aquaculture Cluster in Busan / Courtesy of GS E&C Atlantic salmon require cold, clean water, making precise temperature and water quality control essential for stable year-round farming. To meet such conditions, Eco Aquafarm uses Recirculating Aquaculture System based on GS E&C’s water treatment technologies, so that the water can be continuously filtered and reused. The facility also applies Zero Water Concept technology, which enables up to 99 percent of the water to be reused, creating a more sustainable environment for land-based salmon farming. Salmon hatch in freshwater before growing in seawater, requiring the hatching and smolt stages to take place in freshwater while adult salmon are raised in seawater. This requires advanced ICT-based smart farming technologies to precisely control water temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen levels and quality to maintain optimal growing conditions. Based on its cooling and precision temperature control systems, Eco Aquafarm maintained water temperatures between 12 and 16 degrees Celsius, optimal for raising Salmon, even during the summertime. Its Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition system collected, recorded and analyzed facility data through sensors while automatically adjusting equipment based on real-time water quality monitoring. The technologies developed by GS E&C and Eco Aquafarm resulted in multiple patents. The companies secured patents related to recirculating aquaculture facilities in 2023 and desalination-based aquaculture facilities in 2025. They have also filed a patent for technology that uses underwater cameras to determine when salmon should be transferred to the next stage of their growing environment. “By raising Atlantic salmon at the cluster, we have built technological and operational capabilities across the entire land-based farming process, from water treatment to growth management and facility operations,” a GS E&C official said. “Based on the technologies and data we have accumulated, we will continue to enhance the competitiveness of our land-based aquaculture platform.” Nam Hyun-woo has worked as a staff writer at The Korea Times since 2013, mostly covering business and politics. He currently belongs to the Business Desk where he covers topics such as emerging tech, AI, ICT and Korea's chaebol community. Prior to joining the team, he was the paper's correspondent for the presidential office of Korea during the Yoon Suk Yeol and Moon Jae-in administrations.
